name: Stem cell hair therapy
lead: Stem cell hair therapy is an umbrella term for treatments that inject or apply cells, or products derived from cells, to the scalp in order to slow hair loss or promote regrowth. Variants include adipose-derived (fat) stem cell preparations, stromal vascular fraction, cells cultured from a patient's own hair follicles, donor mesenchymal stem cells, and cell-conditioned extracts or secretomes. [3][7][1][8]

The appeal for appearance is direct: if miniaturised follicles can be supported or reawakened, scalp density and hairline coverage could improve without the donor-area limits of a hair transplant. Clinics that offer such procedures say the cells release growth factors that signal follicles to re-enter the growth phase. Researchers are testing these ideas in small registered trials, many of them early phase or without a control comparison. [3][7][8]

Wikipedia notes that as of 2024 the only FDA-approved stem-cell therapy is hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and that hundreds of US clinics have sold mostly unproven stem-cell treatments, with the FDA and FTC taking enforcement action against some. [11] Hair-loss treatments with the strongest track record, such as minoxidil, finasteride, dutasteride and transplantation, are described separately in general references on hair loss. [12]

paras: The label covers several different procedures. Some use a patient's own fat, processed into stromal vascular fraction or cultured adipose-derived cells; some multiply mesenchymal cells taken from the patient's hair follicles; others use donor cells or cell-free extracts from donor cell cultures. [7][3][8][1] Related but distinct entries on this wiki cover exosomes and hair cloning (culturing follicle-forming cells for implantation).

Autologous approaches involve a harvest step, for example a small fat sample or a scalp punch, followed by laboratory or chairside processing and injection into the scalp. Allogeneic approaches use cells or extracts from donors, which removes the harvest but raises questions about immune compatibility and product standardisation. [1][8] Some clinics combine cells with platelet-rich plasma, and one registered study compared the two after follicular unit extraction. [7][9]

sections.h: Background: stem cells and the follicle
paras: Stem cells are cells that can renew themselves and give rise to specialised cell types; mesenchymal stem cells, found in tissues such as bone marrow and fat, are the type most often used in cosmetic and orthopaedic clinics. [11] The hair follicle itself contains a stem cell population in the bulge region that drives the cycling of the follicle between growth and rest, and a general reference on hair loss links DNA damage in follicle stem cells to follicle miniaturisation. [12]

Researchers have studied follicle-associated stem cells in the laboratory for other purposes, including nerve repair in mice and the behaviour of follicle stem cells in skin tumour models. [14][13] Those studies are not hair-regrowth trials.

Proponents describe the cells acting less by becoming new follicles than by secreting growth factors and signalling vesicles that influence the cells around them, which is why cell-free secretome and exosome preparations are also being tested. [10][11] Wikipedia's overview of stem-cell therapy likewise lists exosomes and secretome products as stem-cell-derived alternatives studied for possibly lower immunogenicity and tumour risk. [11]

For hair, the working hypothesis is that these signals could lengthen the growth phase of miniaturised follicles and improve the local blood supply and extracellular environment. Researchers in the registered trials measure outcomes such as hair counts and density, but results from most of the registrations below are not cited here. [1][3][7]

Small trials have been registered for stem-cell-based hair treatment, though no published results from them are cited in this article. A completed 38-person study tested an allogeneic adipose stem cell component extract in androgenetic alopecia [1]. A completed study of 50 people tested autologous hair-follicle-derived mesenchymal stem cell suspension [3], and a completed phase 2 study of 22 people tested adipose-derived stem cells combined with platelet-rich plasma [7].

Other registrations include a 70-person phase 1/2 study of allogeneic mesenchymal stem cells for androgenetic alopecia [8], a phase 4 comparison of adipose-derived stem cells versus platelet-rich plasma after follicular unit extraction (n=40) [9], a study of 'Stem Cell Educator' therapy in alopecia areata (n=20) [5], a 60-person regeneration study in androgenetic alopecia [6], and a trial of umbilical cord stem cell exosomes (n=50) [10]. A registration for secretome treatment in facial rejuvenation (n=24) shows the same cell-derived approach being tested on skin. [2]

Wikipedia describes one case report of improved hair density after combined CD34+ and umbilical cord stem cell treatment over 12 weeks, and cautions that a single case offers limited evidence. [11] Registration on ClinicalTrials.gov does not mean a study has been reviewed or approved. [11]

Wikipedia reports that clinics selling unapproved stem-cell treatments typically charge $10,000 to $20,000, that insurance generally does not cover them, and that the FTC in 2018 ordered some clinics to pay refunds of about $500,000 for unsubstantiated claims. [11] It also reports FDA lawsuits seeking injunctions against firms selling unapproved adipose-derived products, a 2018 FDA warning letter to a clinic company, and infections in at least 20 US patients after cord-blood products marketed as stem-cell treatments in 2021. [11] These reports concern stem-cell clinics generally rather than hair treatment specifically.

Wikipedia also records that a first wave of clinics appeared in the early 2000s, that medical-tourism clinics followed by 2012, and that by 2016 more than 550 US clinics were selling mostly unproven therapies. [11] Registered trials describe their own safety monitoring; autologous procedures carry the usual risks of harvest and scalp injection, such as pain, bruising and infection.

Stem cell treatment comes up in hair-loss discussions as a possible next step beyond medication and transplants. A T Nation forum user in a 2020 thread about hair loss said he had tried 'every single hair loss treatment', including stem cells twice, and described one of those options as a waste of money while crediting dutasteride for his crown. [16] Posts like this are individual accounts rather than controlled results.

Other forum discussion of stem cells on that site centres on whether clinical trials are needed before clinics sell them; one participant wrote that proper trials are the only way to know whether stem cells work for a given disease. [15]

timeline.event: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation begins to be used for blood cancers; it remains the only FDA-approved stem-cell therapy as of 2024. [11]
Registered study of allogeneic adipose stem cell component extract in androgenetic alopecia begins (n=38). [1]
FTC orders refunds from stem-cell clinics over unsubstantiated claims. [11]
Registered study of autologous hair-follicle-derived mesenchymal cell suspension begins (n=50). [3]
Registrations for an allogeneic mesenchymal stem cell study (2024) and an umbilical cord exosome trial (2024) in androgenetic alopecia. [8][10]

lore.intro: In hair-loss communities stem cells are discussed as a possible future or premium option, with few first-hand reports and frequent calls for proper trials. [16][15]

claims.claim: Stem cell injections can regrow thinning hair
claims.believers: Clinics and some users say cell-derived growth factors reawaken miniaturised follicles and thicken the scalp. [3][7]
claims.experts: Small registered trials exist, but results are not established in the sources cited here, and Wikipedia notes that only HSCT is FDA-approved as stem-cell therapy. [1][11]

claims.claim: Own-fat (autologous) cells are safer than donor cells
claims.believers: Proponents of autologous preparations say using one's own tissue avoids donor-matching questions. [7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia states that autologous harvesting generally involves the least risk of stem-cell sources, while the FDA has taken action against unapproved adipose products. [11]

claims.claim: Stem cells improve results when combined with PRP or transplants
claims.believers: Some clinics pair cells with platelet-rich plasma or offer them after follicular unit extraction. [7][9]
claims.experts: A phase 4 registration compares adipose cells with PRP after follicular unit extraction, and published outcomes are not cited here. [9]

card.summary: Clinic injections of fat-derived or follicle-derived cells for hair regrowth; small trials registered, no approved product.
card.aka: Adipose stem cell hair treatment, SVF hair restoration
card.note: Wikipedia reports regulator action against unapproved stem-cell clinics; costs often run $10,000+.

quick.overview:
Stem cell hair therapy covers procedures that place cells or cell-derived products into the scalp to counter hair loss. Sources include a patient's fat, hair follicle cells or donor mesenchymal cells.

Small trials are registered, but no published results are cited here and no such treatment is FDA-approved for hair loss.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say the cells secrete growth factors that stimulate dormant follicles. In the cited sources this is a proposed mechanism under study in early trials.
quick.risks: Wikipedia reports FDA and FTC action against clinics selling unapproved stem-cell treatments, and serious infections after some cell products in 2021 (not hair-specific). Costs are commonly high and insurance typically does not cover them.

chain: Cells or cell-derived factors are prepared from fat, follicles or donor tissue
Preparation is injected into or applied to the thinning scalp
Growth signals are proposed to support follicles and increase density
angle.text: People pursue it to thicken thinning areas or support a transplant without relying only on remaining donor hair. The proposed route is paracrine signalling from the cells to follicles, which researchers are testing in small trials.
